Donald H. Benton, Duke's Vice President-Marketing, said the "Energy Efficient Structure (EES) program will also help reduce the utility's need to build new generating facilities, a major factor affecting the cost of electricity."
Waste may occur when energy is consumed at a cost greater than the value of that energy to consumers as measured by what they would be willing to pay for it; consequently, proper design of rates may be essential if waste is to be avoided or reduced. Thus rate revision has also been advocated as a means of accomplishing conservation. A function of prices in competitive markets is to guide scarce resources into their most productive uses. Thus, if electric utility rates are set in accordance with competitive market pricing principles, such rates would function in the regulated electric industry to attract only such resources to the industry as would not be more productive elsewhere in the economy.
The hourly, daily, and seasonal variation in load is associated with varying costs. An important objective of peak-load pricing or time-of-day rates, is to give consumers the correct cost-base price "signals" to guide their use of electricity. Clearly there are costs of having rates which vary over time, such as more complex meters, but to the extent that the benefits of peak load pricing exceeds its costs, there is a basis for electric rates relecting variation in system costs during the day and during the year.
Most retail electric rate schedules reflect primarily average running costs and average historical capacity costs. Thus, at peak demand periods the price of electricity may be too low compared to the costs of supplying electricity at such times. As a result, consumption of electric energy may be encouraged, requiring the installation of generating facilities that otherwise would not be required.
The extent to which peak load pricing can be economically justified for any given system depends in part on: (1) customer responses to a revised rate structure, (2) the load characteristics of the system, (3) the ability of the system to flatten its load curve by way of intersystem sales, and (4) the costs and inconvenience of new metering and billing.
